newsitem.title: UK: IRA claims Lisburn bomb, N.Ireland back at brink.
newsitem.headline: IRA claims Lisburn bomb, N.Ireland back at brink.

text.p: The IRA admitted on Tuesday to bombing Britain's Northern Ireland army base, pushing the province back towards the darkest days of its political and sectarian strife.
The Irish Republican Army said in a statement that it had carried out the attack to press its claim for a seat for its Sinn Fein political arm at Northern Ireland peace talks.
British Prime Minister John Major said, however, that the IRA admission was sickening and justified Britain's refusal to invite Sinn Fein to the talks until the IRA declares a ceasefire.
"Sinn Fein have excluded themselves more clearly than ever," said Major from Bournemouth, where his embattled Conservative Party is holding a final pre-election annual conference.
The attack was viewed by security forces and the British government as the most serious development in Northern Ireland since Britain and Ireland launched a peace initiative in 1993.
The IRA's admission appeared to signal a new offensive in Northern Ireland itself after a nine-month campaign directed against the British mainland and an army base in Germany.
Major, his Irish partners in a two-year peace quest and the U.S. government appealed to the IRA's Protestant Loyalist foes not to break their own two-year truce and avenge the IRA attack.
"The Provisional IRA are trying to provoke a general return to violence in Northern Ireland. We must not let them succeed. I appeal to all Loyalists not to fall into this trap," Major said.
His appeal was echoed by spokesmen for the Loyalists' political representatives, who are taking part in Belfast peace talks by virtue of the guerrillas' two-year truce.
"We should avoid as best we can the cycle of violence that undoubtedly would take us to hell and back again," David Ervine of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) told Reuters.
He appealed to the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), the Loyalists' umbrella group, not to endorse a return to the sectarian attacks which killed 900 Catholics prior to the truce.
"I say very, very clearly that the Combined Loyalist Military Command should not be provoked, should not do what their enemy wants them to do," Ervine said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's national security adviser, Anthony Lake, issued a similar appeal from Washington, saying that any Loyalist attack "would be a tragic, tragic decision".

Clinton has thrown his weight behind Anglo-Irish attempts to get all parties, including Sinn Fein, to the conference table to negotiate a settlement between pro-British Protestant Unionist parties and pro-Irish Catholic nationalists.
The governments have stuck to their refusal to invite Sinn Fein until the IRA declares a truce but the IRA has accused them of trying to disarm Republican guerrilla units using the talks as a cover.

"The resolution of the conflict demands an inclusive negotiated settlement. This is not possible unless and until the British Government faces up to its responsibilities," the IRA statement, issued to Irish media, said.

It accused Major of "squandering" its 17-month ceasefire which was dogged by arguments over Britain's insistence that the guerrillas start to disarm to show good faith. In February this year, after the IRA resumed its war with an attack on a complex in the London docklands, Britain changed tack and said the IRA could disarm in stages as talks progressed.
But the IRA said it would accept no preconditions whatsoever and its Tuesday statement repeated previous allegations against Major's government.
"The blame for the failure thus far of the Irish peace initiative lies squarely with John Major and his Government," it said.
